questions.question: What is critical reading mainly about?
options: Evaluating how and why a text tries to influence the reader
Reading as fast as possible
Finding spelling mistakes in the text
Memorising the text word for word
questions.explanation: Critical reading goes beyond understanding what a text says — you analyse the author's purpose, techniques and what is left out.

questions.question: A text uses many statistics and references to research. Which persuasive appeal is this?
options: Logos
Pathos
Ethos
Bandwagon
questions.explanation: Statistics and research appeal to logic — logos. Emotional stories are pathos; references to authority are ethos.

questions.question: What is the "bandwagon" technique?
options: Claiming that "everyone else is doing it" to persuade you
Using a celebrity to sell a product
Repeating the same word many times
Quoting scientific studies
questions.explanation: Bandwagon persuades by suggesting that everyone else already agrees or participates, so you should too.

questions.question: What distinguishes synthesis from summary?
options: Synthesis combines insights from several sources; summary retells one source
Synthesis is shorter than summary
Summary requires several sources; synthesis only one
There is no difference
questions.explanation: A summary retells what one source says, while a synthesis combines several sources to create new, deeper understanding of a topic.

questions.question: If a text uses persuasive techniques, what should a critical reader conclude?
options: Recognise the techniques and evaluate the content — the text is not necessarily false
Reject the text immediately as propaganda
Accept it since techniques show skill
Stop reading after the first paragraph
questions.explanation: A text can use persuasive techniques and still be true. Critical reading is about recognising the techniques, not automatically rejecting the information.
